strengths: Rigorous continuous-time analysis with explicit dimension-dependence: Theorem 3.1 provides clean, traceable conditions for dimension-uniform bounds on ALD sampling error.

Novel insight on necessity of preconditioning: The paper identifies that preconditioning is not just helpful but necessary for dimension-robust stability under score errors. Conditions (77)-(79) make this mechanism explicit.
Systematic error decomposition: Proposition 4.1 cleanly separates initialization error, score error, and annealing bias, enabling independent analysis of each component.

Elegant infinite-dimensional framework: Formulating via truncations of an infinite-dimensional target is conceptually cleaner than fixing dimension and facilitates meaningful cross-dimension comparison.
Comprehensive theoretical treatment: Proofs are careful and complete, including challenging components like the responsibility-mismatch analysis in Section B.3.
Theory validated numerically: Figures 3-4 directly demonstrate the predicted effect of spectral design and preconditioning on KL divergence, showing the theory is not vacuous.
weaknesses: Restricted to diagonal Gaussian mixtures: Analysis assumes diagonal covariances and co-diagonalizability, which is essential for calculations but severely limits applicability. Extensions to non-diagonal or general covariances are unclear.

No discretization error analysis: Paper analyzes only continuous-time ALD; discretization (required in practice) is acknowledged but not theoretically addressed. Standard analysis suggests errors could scale as O(d·Δt), potentially destroying dimension-uniformity.

Initialization cost unaddressed: Theorem 3.1 assumes exact sampling from ρ₀ᵈ (a heavy-tailed mixture). The cost of this initialization in high dimensions is not quantified and could dominate total cost.

Artificial error model: Assumption 4.2 models score error as perturbations to a diagonal Gaussian mixture. Realistic learned scores (e.g., neural networks) may not satisfy this structure, limiting practical relevance.

Sufficient conditions are very complex: Equations (77)-(79) involve multiple coupled summability conditions on (γⱼ, λⱼ, σᵢⱼ, Δmᵢⱼ, Δσᵢⱼ) that are hard to verify in practice. No simple worked examples demonstrating all conditions hold simultaneously.

Limited experimental validation: Section 5 tests only on synthetic diagonal GMMs with no comparison to baselines (parallel tempering, other annealing schemes, classical Langevin). No timing comparisons or evidence of practical advantage.
Missing discretization-algorithm gap: Experiments use finite Δt and N but theory only covers continuous-time limit. Consistency between theoretical guarantees and finite-time algorithm is unclear.

strengths: First rigorous dimension-uniform convergence analysis for ALD on multimodal targets, improving upon polynomial dependence results in prior work
Comprehensive theoretical analysis including exact conditions for dimension-uniform control (condition 6) and detailed perturbative analysis for score and initialization errors
Clear identification of preconditioning's role in preventing coordinatewise error accumulation across dimensions
Well-motivated infinite-dimensional perspective connecting to classical function-space sampling theory
Technically sound proofs using appropriate tools (path-space KL, Girsanov's formula) with complete appendices
Convincing experimental validation demonstrating predicted dimension dependence and robustness to neighborhood size choices
weaknesses: Restriction to diagonal Gaussian mixtures significantly limits applicability; no quantitative analysis of approximation quality when using sufficiently many components
Complex sufficient conditions (e.g., equations 57-63) lack practical design guidance; unclear how practitioners should choose Γᵈ and Cᵈ for problems outside the assumed structure

Requires exact initialization from smoothed distribution ρ⁰ᵈ and access to exact time-dependent scores; perturbative analysis assumes small relative perturbations (ρ_tail < 1/9) without discussing robustness beyond this regime
Essential dependence on companion discretization analysis (Baldassari et al., 2026a) for practical applicability; paper alone provides limited guidance on implementation
Limited experimental scope (only bimodal Gaussian mixtures, d ≤ 75); no comparison to alternative multimodal samplers or demonstration on genuinely non-Gaussian or inverse problems

Component means do not appear in dimension-uniform condition (6), which is counterintuitive and inadequately explained; characterization of preconditioning trade-off with discretization requirements lacks quantification

strengths: Well-motivated problem: addresses a genuine gap in dimension-uniform sampling guarantees for multimodal distributions in infinite dimensions
Comprehensive technical analysis: covers exact scores, perturbative regimes with score/initialization errors, and provides explicit spectral conditions for dimension-uniformity
Explicit characterization of sufficient conditions (Eq. 6) rather than mere existence results, enabling principled design of smoothing covariance and preconditioner
Solid proof techniques: careful tracking of dimension dependence, thorough decomposition of error sources (annealing-induced bias, score mismatch, initialization error)
Novel insight on preconditioning: shows that preconditioner with sufficiently decaying spectrum is essential for preventing high-frequency error accumulation, not just for acceleration
weaknesses: Severely restrictive model: analysis limited to diagonal Gaussian mixtures with covariances diagonal in the same basis. Claim that this approximates general mixtures is weak—the analysis does not handle approximation error or non-diagonal targets

Continuous-time analysis only with unresolved discrete-time gap: authors acknowledge that Euler–Maruyama introduces 'additional high-frequency constraints absent from continuous-time theory, limiting applicability.' Practitioners use discrete algorithms, not continuous diffusions

Unverifiable conditions in practice: condition (6) requires knowing component covariance spectra σ_ij to design γ_j and λ_j. No practical procedure provided for parameter selection when true target is unknown

Limited novelty: directly adapts path-space analysis from Guo et al. (2025) to dimension-uniform setting; perturbative analysis uses standard techniques. Main contribution is problem-setting rather than methodological innovation

Weak experimental validation: only toy bimodal Gaussian mixtures that exactly match model assumptions; no realistic high-dimensional multimodal problems; no comparison with baselines (replica exchange, parallel tempering); no demonstration of parameter selection in practice

Stringent and unverifiable assumptions: Assumption 4.2 (perturbations preserve mixture structure) is specific; perturbation bounds ρ ∈ (0, 1/9) are restrictive; low-mode conditions (57–60) require case-by-case verification for each mode

Hidden constants in bounds: dimension-uniformity may be vacuous if constants (β_*, C_j, C_tail) are large. No empirical verification that constants are reasonable or that empirical time horizons match theoretical bounds
Incomplete problem characterization: paper does not identify natural problem classes where condition (6) is satisfied, nor when it fails; no guidance on robustness to condition violations

strengths: Rigorous theoretical analysis establishing dimension-uniform sampling guarantees for ALD on Gaussian mixtures—bridging a gap between empirical success and existing pessimistic bounds. Theorem 3.1 provides explicit, verifiable spectral conditions (Eq. 6).

Comprehensive perturbative theory (Section 4, Propositions B.5–B.7) showing that preconditioner spectral decay prevents error accumulation across coordinates. This is substantially more developed than prior work.

Elegant problem formulation in Hilbert space with finite-dimensional truncations, connecting naturally to infinite-dimensional function-space sampling theory and enabling principled preconditioning design.

Strong mathematical technique: path-matching energy approach (Eq. 5) cleverly isolates annealing bias; factorization of moment bounds over coordinates (Eq. 41) reduces infinite sums to manageable conditions.

Convincing experimental illustrations (Figures 1, 3–4) showing that spectral design genuinely matters for dimension-robustness, not merely a proof artifact. Robustness checks (Appendix D.6) add credibility.
Honest treatment of limitations: authors explicitly acknowledge restrictions (co-diagonalizability, Gaussian mixtures, discretization deferred) rather than overstating applicability.
Clear presentation with well-motivated introduction, logical organization, and detailed appendices. Implementation details in Section D facilitate reproducibility.
weaknesses: Restrictive structural assumptions significantly limit scope: diagonal covariances, co-diagonalizability of component covariances/smoothing/preconditioner. While justified, these exclude many natural problems.

Gap between continuous-time theory and practice: Theorem 3.1 does not apply to Euler–Maruyama discretization. Authors acknowledge discretization imposes additional constraints absent from theory; deferring to companion paper leaves practitioners uncertain whether guarantees survive time-stepping.

Perturbative conditions (Proposition B.7) are complex and restrictive: condition (61) allows only ~11% relative error (ρ_tail < 1/9), and condition (63) on pairwise score variation is not immediately interpretable or easy to verify in practice.

Initialization cost is unquantified: Theorem 3.1 assumes exact sampling from ρ₀^d. Cost of sampling from the smoothed law—especially when smoothing is weak—is acknowledged but not analyzed, potentially negating annealing benefits.

Limited experimental scope: only bimodal Gaussian mixtures tested up to d=75; targets with K≥3 components, higher dimensions (d≥200), and non-power-law spectra would strengthen claims. No comparison to alternative samplers (replica-exchange, parallel tempering, etc.).

Lack of practical design guidance: given a target problem, how should practitioners choose λⱼ and γⱼ? Trade-off between annealing-bias control and perturbative stability is noted but not resolved into actionable design principles.
Infinite-dimensional target requirement limits applicability: framework assumes explicit ρ^∞_⋆ with known spectral properties, unavailable for empirical or learned targets.
Only linear annealing schedule analyzed in detail despite claims of extension to other schedules; adaptive or optimized schedules not explored despite potential computational benefits.
